strengths: Practical and timely task formulation: Exploring forensic surveillance search through multimodal queries (reference image of a person of interest plus a textual question) addresses a significant real-world challenge that existing generic video QA benchmarks do not adequately cover.

Comprehensive benchmark design: ForeSeaQA incorporates joint evaluation of answer accuracy and temporal localization (IoU) across six forensic subtasks, with carefully constructed negative pairs for person search and manual verification of generated QA pairs.

Well-motivated person-centric pipeline: Combining object tracking, unified multimodal embedding (VISTA), and VideoLLM reasoning provides a strong inductive bias that effectively reduces the search space and improves both retrieval latency and QA performance compared to dense video processing.

Thorough empirical evaluation and analysis: The paper benchmarks a wide spectrum of foundation models (LLaVA-OneVision, GLM-4.1V, InternVL3, Qwen2.5-VL, VideoLLaMA3) and RAG methods, backed by insightful ablations on spatial grounding strategies (crops vs. overlays vs. coordinate prompts) and cross-domain generalization on VideoMME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: ForeSea primarily chains existing off-the-shelf components (YOLO + ByteTrack, pre-trained VISTA encoder, and VideoLLaMA3) in a modular pipeline rather than introducing new learning objectives or model architectures.

Dataset scale and domain diversity: ForeSeaQA consists of 1,041 QA pairs derived exclusively from UCF-Crime videos. While suitable as a proof-of-concept diagnostic benchmark, the total scale is relatively modest and restricted to a single source dataset with specific surveillance camera qualities and distributions.

Low absolute temporal localization scores: Across all evaluated models, temporal localization IoU remains quite low (~7–18%), and ForeSea-Global actually outperforms ForeSea on temporal IoU (16.1% vs 13.8%), indicating that person-centric track segment retrieval can sometimes truncate necessary temporal context for events and activities.

Lack of details on dataset quality control: While the paper notes that QA pairs underwent manual verification, it lacks quantitative statistics on verification effort, such as initial hallucination/error rates of the LLM pipeline, rejection rates, or inter-annotator agreement.

strengths: Practical and well-motivated problem: Answering multimodal queries (reference image + question) with precise temporal localization represents a critical, underexplored requirement in AI forensic surveillance.

Benchmark contribution (ForeSeaQA): The proposed benchmark thoughtfully formalizes joint question answering and temporal localization across six diverse forensic subtasks (search, activity, event, temporal, counting, anomaly), backed by a semi-automated pipeline with human verification.

Comprehensive experimental comparison: The paper benchmarks a wide range of recent open-weight Video LMMs (from 2B up to 72B parameters) and Video-RAG frameworks, clearly demonstrating the specific difficulty of multimodal queries and temporal grounding in long surveillance videos.

Practical efficiency and domain transfer: ForeSea demonstrates competitive retrieval and generation latency (2.6s total inference time) while demonstrating strong generalizability on general-purpose long video benchmarks (VideoMME, MLVU, LongVideoBench) with reduced frame budgets.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty in the ForeSea framework: The method primarily chains off-the-shelf components (YOLO + ByteTrack for person tracking, VISTA/GCL for multimodal embedding, and VideoLLaMA3 for generation) without proposing new foundational retrieval or multimodal fusion architectures.

Dataset scale and video diversity: ForeSeaQA comprises 1,041 questions derived exclusively from the UCF-Crime dataset. While human-verified, evaluating on a single surveillance source limits the diversity of camera perspectives, resolutions, and environmental domains.

Trade-off between person-centric tracking and temporal localization: As shown in Table 2 and Table 6, ForeSea-Global consistently outperforms person-centric ForeSea in temporal localization IoU (e.g., 16.1% vs. 13.8% on ForeSeaQAMM, and 18.6% vs. 13.3% on text queries), indicating that person tracking/filtering can truncate broader temporal context necessary for precise event boundaries.

Low overall temporal IoU: Across all evaluated models, temporal localization IoUs remain quite low (mostly 7–16%), suggesting that extracting fine-grained temporal boundaries from retrieved candidate tracks remains an open, challenging problem that the current prompting pipeline does not fully resolve.

strengths: Relevant and practical problem formulation: Searching surveillance footage using multimodal queries (combining a reference photo of an individual with natural language questions) with joint temporal grounding reflects real-world forensic needs that are underserved by existing text-only video QA benchmarks.

Comprehensive benchmark design: ForeSeaQA incorporates six distinct subtasks (search, activity, event, temporal, counting, anomaly) with both text and multimodal query variants, complemented by manual validation of generated QA pairs.

Thorough evaluation: The authors evaluate multiple competitive open-source Video LMMs (from 2B up to 72B parameters) and VideoRAG methods, alongside latency/throughput analysis and testing on standard long-video benchmarks (VideoMME, MLVU, LongVideoBench).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: The proposed ForeSea framework is entirely a cascading pipeline of existing, pre-trained off-the-shelf tools (YOLOv5 + ByteTrack for person tracking, pre-trained VISTA/GCL for multimodal embedding, and off-the-shelf VideoLLaMA3 for generation). There is no newly proposed architecture, training objective, or loss function.

Mixed empirical support for the person-centric inductive bias: A central claim of the paper is that person-centric tracking and indexing are crucial. However, the ablations show that 'ForeSea-Global' (which bypasses human tracking and indexes full frames) achieves a higher temporal IoU (16.1% vs. 13.8% on multimodal queries; 18.6% vs. 13.3% on text queries) and even higher overall text accuracy (68.1% vs. 66.7%). This undermines the central narrative that person-centric tracking is superior.

Relatively small benchmark size: ForeSeaQA consists of only 1,041 QA pairs across all six subtasks, which translates to fewer than 200 questions per task. Furthermore, all videos originate from a single source dataset (UCF-Crime), limiting scenario diversity (e.g., camera viewpoints, resolution, lighting).

Metric inflation in temporal localization for the Search task: As detailed in Appendix C.3, for negative pairs in the search task, temporal IoU is set to 1 if both ground truth and prediction are negative. Because search contains balanced positive/negative pairs, predicting negative heavily inflates the reported temporal IoU scores, which can distort the true temporal boundary precision.

Discrepancies in system description: Section 4.3 states that candidate clips have bounding boxes drawn on every frame ('draw bbox on every frame' - visual overlay), but Section 5.3 and Table 2 indicate that the best performing and default configuration actually passes bounding boxes as textual coordinates in the prompt without visual overlay (Crop=X, Overlay=X, Coords=V). This creates confusion regarding the exact pipeline used in the primary results.

strengths: Addresses a highly practical and underexplored challenge in video surveillance: answering multimodal forensic queries (e.g., reference image of a person of interest paired with text questions) with temporally grounded evidence.

Introduces ForeSeaQA, a well-structured benchmark covering six distinct forensic subtasks (search, activity, event, temporal, counting, anomaly) with dual evaluation across multiple-choice accuracy and temporal IoU under both text-only and multimodal query settings.

Rigorous data curation process incorporating multiple verification steps: dense caption extraction, multimodal LLM visual grounding, and two-stage manual and automated validation to filter noise and hallucinated coordinates.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation comparing against a wide spectrum of modern Video LMMs (up to 72B) and VideoRAG baselines, supported by detailed ablations on spatial grounding modalities (crop vs. overlay vs. text coordinates), retriever encoders, and backbone VLMs.

Demonstrates strong computational efficiency (2.6 s total latency vs. 3.8–7.6 s for baselines) and surprising generalization to general long-video benchmarks (VideoMME, MLVU, LongVideoBench) at a fraction of the frame budget.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is relatively incremental: the proposed ForeSea framework primarily integrates existing off-the-shelf tools (YOLO/ByteTrack, GCL/VISTA multimodal encoder, and VideoLLaMA3) into a standard retrieve-then-generate pipeline without introducing fundamentally new model architectures or training objectives.
The benchmark scale is somewhat modest (1,041 curated QA pairs), especially compared to broader video understanding benchmarks, which may limit the diversity of edge-case scenarios.

While the motivation highlights multi-camera surveillance environments, the tracking and retrieval pipelines are evaluated primarily on single-camera video streams from UCF-Crime without true cross-camera association or re-identification mechanisms.

Temporal localization IoU numbers across all models remain quite low in absolute terms (~10–18%), indicating that temporal boundary precision remains largely unresolved. Furthermore, setting temporal IoU to 1.0 when both ground-truth and prediction are negative (no event) in the binary search subtask may potentially inflate localization metrics.

strengths: Practical and timely problem: Addressing forensic search in long surveillance footage using multimodal queries (reference image + question) and requiring joint answer accuracy and temporal localization is highly relevant for real-world surveillance operations.

Well-designed benchmark (ForeSeaQA): The proposed benchmark incorporates multimodal queries across six diverse subtasks (search, activity, event, temporal, counting, anomaly) with explicit timestamped groundings, backed by a rigorous semi-automated pipeline and human verification.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper evaluates an extensive range of native Video LMMs (up to 72B) and retrieval-augmented baselines (VideoRAG, T*), presenting thorough ablations on grounding formats (crop vs. overlay vs. textual coordinates), retrieval top-K, and multimodal encoders.

Solid efficiency and transferability: ForeSea achieves lower inference latency (2.6s) than full-video LMMs and prior RAG baselines, and transfers effectively to general long-video benchmarks (VideoMME, MLVU, LongVideoBench) with reduced frame budgets.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is somewhat modest: ForeSea is largely an engineering integration of existing off-the-shelf components (ByteTrack/YOLO, GCL/VISTA/SigLIP, VideoLLaMA3/LLaVA-Video) rather than introducing novel learning objectives or model architectures.

Benchmark scale: While the curation and human verification pipeline is thorough, ForeSeaQA contains 1,041 questions in total, which is relatively modest in scale compared to modern video QA benchmarks.

Multi-camera setup not fully realized: Although the introduction emphasizes forensic search across long, multi-camera networks, the benchmark and experimental validation are primarily built upon single-video clips from UCF-Crime, without explicitly evaluating cross-camera association or re-identification across non-overlapping views.

Mixed performance on text queries: Table 1 reveals that against the native VideoLLaMA3-7B baseline, ForeSea actually achieves slightly lower accuracy (66.7% vs. 67.7%) and lower temporal IoU (13.3% vs. 15.5%) on text-only queries (ForeSeaQA-Text), indicating that the gains are primarily confined to multimodal queries.

strengths: Practical and well-motivated problem: Combining reference person crops with natural language queries for temporal forensic search addresses a clear operational need in video surveillance that standard text-only video QA benchmarks overlook.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation and ablations: The authors evaluate a wide range of recent open-source Video LMMs (VideoLLaMA3, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, LLaVA-Video) and conduct thorough ablations comparing spatial guidance representations (cropping, bounding box overlay, textual coordinates) and retrieval scopes (person-centric, global, hybrid).

Efficiency benefits: The paper convincingly demonstrates that person-centric retrieval reduces the temporal context window passed to the Video LMM, cutting inference latency while preserving or slightly improving question-answering accuracy.
weaknesses: Limited technical and algorithmic originality: The proposed ForeSea framework is fundamentally a modular pipeline connecting existing off-the-shelf tools (YOLOv5 + ByteTrack for tracking, off-the-shelf multimodal encoders like GCL/VISTA/SigLIP for retrieval, and VideoLLaMA3/LLaVA-Video for generation). No new learning objectives, architectures, or retrieval-generation interaction mechanisms are introduced.

Small benchmark scale and reliance on semi-automated generation: ForeSeaQA contains only 1,041 question-answer pairs derived from UCF-Crime videos. Given the rapid scaling of video-language benchmarks, ~1k questions across six subtasks is relatively small, limiting the statistical diversity and robustness of the evaluation.

Extremely low temporal localization performance across all models: Across all evaluated models and configurations, temporal localization IoU remains very low (roughly 10%–16% average IoU, with subtask scores frequently below 5%). This indicates either severe limitations in current models' temporal grounding capabilities or potential alignment/granularity issues in how ground-truth intervals are defined and scored.

Disconnect in open-domain generalization claims: When evaluating on general video benchmarks (VideoMME, MLVU, LongVideoBench), the framework discards its central premise—person tracking—and falls back to standard uniform frame-level retrieval. On VideoMME, ForeSea actually scores lower than the native VideoLLaMA3 baseline (65.6% vs. 66.2%), weakening the claim of broad architectural superiority beyond the specific domain.

Lack of tracking failure analysis: Surveillance videos frequently present heavy occlusions, low resolution, motion blur, and ID switches. The manuscript does not systematically evaluate how tracking failures or missed detections propagate downstream into retrieval and final QA generation.
